stories.headline: Former IRS Agent Indicted for Laundering Drug Money Through Denver Tax Business
stories.summary:
A federal grand jury has indicted a former IRS agent on 12 counts of money laundering and filing false tax returns after he allegedly used his Denver tax preparation business, Blue Bear Tax Solutions, to disguise drug proceeds as legitimate income. Clinton Roosevelt Dale, 51, is accused of creating fictitious businesses — including registering them with the Colorado Secretary of State's Office — and filing fraudulent returns for clients who were dealing cocaine.

Prosecutors say Dale's scheme served two purposes: allowing drug clients to present false proof of legitimate income when purchasing homes and luxury vehicles, and underreporting taxable income to defraud the IRS. One of the clients for whom Dale allegedly prepared false returns turned out to be an undercover IRS criminal investigation agent.

Dale worked as a contact representative and revenue agent at the IRS for more than a decade before resigning in 2014 rather than face termination over false mileage reimbursements, misuse of a government travel card, and lack of candor, according to the indictment. The alleged fraudulent tax filings covered the period from 2022 through April 2025.

stories.headline: Charges to Be Dropped Against Four Arrested During ICE Protest in Arapahoe County
stories.summary:
The 18th Judicial District announced Thursday that charges against four demonstrators arrested during a July protest outside an Immigration and Customs Enforcement field office in Centennial will be dismissed Friday. Yoselin Corrales, Arnie Carter, El Moss, and Terry Burnsed were each charged with obstructing a passageway; Corrales and Moss also faced charges of obstructing a peace officer.

District Attorney Amy Padden said prosecutors determined the cases should not move forward, citing the First Amendment and prosecutorial discretion. Padden noted the protesters were not violent, did not threaten law enforcement, and did not damage property or disrupt traffic, calling the dismissal "in the interest of justice."

Defense attorney Andy McNulty called the dismissal a move that "respects the First Amendment," but noted that the four defendants still had to hire attorneys and appear in court before charges were dropped. The arrests drew dozens of community supporters to the defendants' arraignments at the Arapahoe County Justice Center on Sept. 9.

stories.headline: Colorado Supreme Court Upholds Vail Resorts Liability Waiver, Dismisses Injured Snowboarder's Lawsuit
stories.summary:
The Colorado Supreme Court ruled 4-3 to dismiss a lawsuit filed by snowboarder John Litterer, who was injured in a December 2020 collision with an employee-driven snowmobile at Breckenridge ski area. The majority found that a liability waiver Litterer signed when purchasing a 2022-23 Epic Pass — while he was already in active litigation with Vail Resorts — released all existing claims against the company.

The court ruled that the landmark Miller case, which established that liability waivers cannot shield resorts from violations of state safety laws, did not apply here because Litterer signed his waiver after his injury, not before. The majority held that anyone who signs a contract is presumed to know its contents, regardless of claimed uncertainty.

Three dissenting justices argued the ruling gives the ski industry an "extraordinary perpetual pass" by allowing resorts to bury sweeping liability language in lengthy click-through boilerplate documents. Justice Richard Gabriel, writing the dissent, called the decision "unjust" and warned it will result in "manifest injustice to innumerable unsuspecting ski pass purchasers." The case had been closely watched by the resort industry following the Miller decision, which resulted in a record $12.4 million award.

stories.headline: East Colfax Bus Rapid Transit Opens Broadway to Colorado Boulevard Segment, More Than a Year Ahead of Schedule
stories.summary:
Denver's East Colfax Bus Rapid Transit project reached a significant milestone this weekend, opening dedicated center bus lanes from Broadway to Colorado Boulevard ahead of Sunday morning service. RTD's 15 and 15L bus routes will now operate in the new middle lanes, stopping at center platforms marked by large white arches, with buses arriving every four to five minutes.

The East Colfax BRT Project Director Jonathan Stewart said the opening is "more than 12 months ahead of schedule." Once the full project is complete — expected around the end of 2027, with service extending into Aurora at I-225 — RTD will launch the Lynx branded BRT service, replacing the existing bus routes entirely. Riders will pay through ticket vending machines at platforms before boarding.

The project has removed parallel parking near the center stations and reduced a section of Colfax from two vehicle lanes to one in each direction, which has divided neighborhood reaction. Some residents and riders welcome the improved transit frequency and visibility for businesses, while others worry about traffic patterns and foot traffic impacts along the corridor.

stories.headline: Colorado to Receive $250 Million in Federal Funds for Colorado-Texas Power Grid Connection
stories.summary:
The U.S. Department of Energy announced a $250 million investment in a transmission project linking Colorado and Texas that officials say will improve grid reliability and help meet growing electricity demand. The Colorado-to-Texas Western-Eastern Intertie Modernization Initiative, known as CO2TX, is part of the Colorado Energy Office's broader $1.2 billion infrastructure effort to bridge energy gaps between regional power interconnections.

The project includes a connection from Lamar to the May Valley substation in Brandon, linking directly to the Colorado Power Pathway transmission network. Xcel Energy, Colorado's largest electric utility, is providing an 80% financing match in addition to the federal grant.

Gov. Jared Polis said the investment means "lower costs and fewer outages for Coloradans" by strengthening the state's ability to share power with other regions during extreme weather and peak demand periods. Federal officials framed the project as part of a national push to secure reliable and affordable energy infrastructure.

stories.headline: Denver Business Leaders Launch 'Denver. The Best Return on Life' Campaign to Counter Negative Economic Narrative
stories.summary:
A coalition of prominent Denver business and civic leaders has launched a grassroots marketing campaign called "Denver. The Best Return on Life," aimed at reframing national perceptions of the city's economy and quality of life. The initiative was organized by developers, hospitality executives, and real estate leaders including Matt Joblon of BMC Investments, Walter Isenberg of Sage Hospitality Group, and Kourtny Garrett of the Downtown Denver Partnership.

The group set out to raise $2.5 million and exceeded its fundraising goal. The campaign will promote Denver's lifestyle amenities, business ecosystem, and major city investments — including the reconstruction of 16th Street, a $100 million job-growth program, and the nearly $1 billion Vibrant Denver bond program — to a national audience.

Mayor Mike Johnston backed the campaign, calling Denver one of the "rare" cities where companies can grow and employees want to live. The effort comes as Colorado has faced criticism about slipping economic competitiveness, and the campaign specifically positions Denver as more affordable than San Francisco and sunnier than San Diego.

stories.headline: Denver 911 Response Times Worsen, Staffing Levels Face Scrutiny in City Budget Hearings
stories.summary:
Denver residents calling 911 are waiting longer for someone to answer, according to reporting that surfaced during the city's annual budget hearings. The deterioration in call-answering performance over the past year has drawn attention from city officials examining staffing levels at the emergency communications center.

The budget process has put a spotlight on whether Denver is adequately funding its 911 operations as the city weighs competing priorities. Details on the extent of the delays and specific staffing shortfalls are being examined as part of the broader budget negotiation process.

The issue has broader public safety implications for a city already navigating concerns about emergency response capacity. City leaders are expected to address 911 staffing as part of finalized budget decisions in the coming weeks.

stories.headline: Driverless Waymo Attempts to Navigate Through Closed Denver Street Construction Near Sloan's Lake
stories.summary:
A driverless Waymo vehicle attempted to drive down a street closed for resurfacing in Denver's West Colfax neighborhood near Sloan's Lake on Thursday, the city's Department of Transportation and Infrastructure confirmed. A photo of the autonomous vehicle facing orange construction cones and three workers circulated widely on social media, coming just days after another Waymo drove through the South Pearl Street farmers market while vendors were setting up.

City transportation spokesperson Nancy Kuhn said the vehicle did not significantly disrupt the resurfacing project near Perry Street and Conejos Place and caused no damage. The department said it plans to work with Waymo to better understand how its vehicles receive traffic and road-closure information and to explore whether additional coordination is possible.

The incident highlights a gap in Colorado law: the state currently has no mechanism to ticket driverless vehicles for traffic violations because there is no driver present. City officials noted that if a Waymo vehicle caused property damage, the city could seek reimbursement from the company or pursue civil litigation.

stories.headline: Pitkin County Approves Plan to Take Over Day-to-Day Management of Maroon Bells Scenic Area
stories.summary:
The Pitkin County Board of County Commissioners has approved a special use permit framework with the U.S. Forest Service that will give the county day-to-day operational oversight of the Maroon Bells Scenic Area beginning with the 2027 season. The agreement creates a dedicated enterprise fund so that fees collected at the site can be directed back into its management, infrastructure, and long-term needs — addressing a persistent funding shortfall.

The site currently generates about $220,000 in annual revenue against operating costs of roughly $600,000, a gap that has limited staffing, constrained amenities, and required financial support from other sources. Some fees, which have remained flat for three decades despite rising costs, are expected to increase under the new model.

The U.S. Forest Service retains ownership and federal stewardship authority over the scenic area, and the special use permit does not involve any transfer of land. The permit is expected to be issued initially for a five-year period, with an option to renew for an additional five years, and public comment on the arrangement opened September 24. Approximately 191,000 people visited the Maroon Bells between May and October last year.

stories.headline: Wolf's Tailor Pop-Up 'Sheep' Extends Through End of 2026 at Cherry Creek Hotel
stories.summary:
Sheep, the pop-up residency from the team behind Colorado's only two-Michelin-star restaurant, The Wolf's Tailor, will continue through the end of 2026 at the Clayton Hotel & Members Club in Denver's Cherry Creek neighborhood. The open-fire tasting menu experience had originally been scheduled to close Oct. 4 but will now run through December, though the price has risen from $95 to $125 per person for the four-course dinner.

The pop-up, which debuted July 8 in the 54-seat rooftop restaurant space — the first time that venue has been opened to the public — is led by Id Est founder Kelly Whitaker and chef Taylor Stark. Dishes have included smoked heirloom tomato jelly, mackerel with tom kha cream, and squab with sourdough gochujang, accompanied by paired seasonal cocktails and wines.

Sheep will operate dinner service only for the remainder of its extended run. The extension marks continued interest in the high-end dining concept and the first sustained public access to the Clayton Hotel's rooftop restaurant space.

stories.headline: Broncos Host Rams on Sunday Night Football in Week 3 With Running Back Room Banged Up
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos will host the Los Angeles Rams in a high-profile Sunday Night Football matchup in Week 3, with Denver entering the game having won nine consecutive games against NFC opponents since quarterback Bo Nix took over in 2024. Nix posted a 9.3 yards-per-dropback average in the team's Week 2 win over Jacksonville, described as Denver's best such figure since the Peyton Manning era.

The Broncos' backfield depth is a concern heading into the game, with running backs J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey both limited in practice with hamstring injuries, and rookie Jonah Coleman missing practice as well. Coleman had been a bright spot through two games, breaking multiple runs of 10 or more yards and scoring a touchdown in the Week 2 victory.

Nix, who grew up watching Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford after Stafford was the No. 1 overall pick in 2009, will face a Los Angeles defense that was significantly upgraded in the offseason. The Rams are regarded as Super Bowl favorites entering the season.

stories.headline: Avalanche Make Additional Roster Cuts Ahead of Sept. 30 Season Opener
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche announced another round of roster cuts this week as the team works toward finalizing its opening-night lineup for the Sept. 30 season opener. A larger-than-usual group remains with the team at this stage, as the Avalanche plan to use several players in a Sept. 26 preseason road game against Utah before making further reductions.

The team is expected to make a significant additional cut after the Utah contest to reach the required opening-night roster size. Colorado enters its new season as a Stanley Cup favorite, according to analysts, and training camp has featured an overhauled supporting cast around star center Nikita Jokic — though that dynamic applies to the Nuggets; the Avalanche are building around their core led by Nathan MacKinnon.

Meanwhile, defenseman Brent Burns has been reported to be targeting the all-time NHL ironman record this season, adding another storyline to the Avalanche's opening weeks.

topStory.headline: Danish Intelligence Warns of Low but Growing Risk of Russian Military Strike on NATO Territory
topStory.summary:
Denmark's Defence Intelligence Service issued one of the starkest warnings yet from a Western security agency on Thursday, cautioning that Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO member countries bordering its territory within the coming months. Intelligence chief Thomas Ahrenkiel described the risk as low but increasing, noting that potential actions could include isolated missile or drone strikes on infrastructure supporting Ukraine, false-flag operations using Ukrainian-made drones, or incursions by small numbers of soldiers potentially operating without identifying insignia.

The Danish assessment also warned that Russia is expected to intensify its broader hybrid warfare campaign against European nations, including destructive cyberattacks targeting critical infrastructure and sabotage operations carrying a high risk of casualties. Potential targets identified in the report include defense manufacturers, transport networks carrying military equipment, and other infrastructure linked to Western support for Ukraine. NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, confirmed Thursday that the alliance was increasing intelligence sharing in response to the threat, urging member states to remain calm while describing recent developments as concerning.

The warning came hours after a fire at a Starlink satellite station in Poland's Masovian voivodeship that Polish Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski described as a deliberate act of sabotage intended to disable the facility and disrupt internet access, including for Ukrainian military users. Gawkowski said responsibility had not been formally established but that the incident bore the hallmarks of what he called Russia's new doctrine of hybrid attack. The incident follows a series of similar events across Europe in recent weeks, including an attempted drone attack on Germany's Leipzig/Halle airport that Berlin has publicly attributed to Russia, as well as fires at drone factories and sabotage of rail infrastructure.

Also on Thursday, Sweden and Finland conducted their first joint fighter jet intercept operation, scrambling aircraft to track and identify a group of Russian military planes, including a transport aircraft and several fighters, flying in international airspace over the Gulf of Finland. Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson called the operation a concrete expression of the readiness and trust built through Nordic and NATO cooperation. The intercept underscored the heightened state of alert across the region as Russian military and covert activity near NATO borders continues to escalate.

The Danish intelligence assessment stops short of asserting that Moscow has approved a specific operation or that an attack is imminent, but it reflects a broader shift in the warnings being issued by European security services. A source familiar with Russian military thinking told The Guardian that Russia's top command believes several NATO countries are directly involved in the war through intelligence sharing and assistance guiding Ukrainian missiles and drones, and therefore considers itself justified in responding with hybrid operations. Whether NATO could agree on a collective response to a limited Russian strike — a scenario the Danish report specifically flags as a potential Russian objective — remains an open question for the alliance.
